source("_common.R")

Every analysis in this guide goes through the same steps. A **question** ("does
smoking cause coronary heart disease, and by how much?") becomes an
**estimand**: a precise quantity, such as the risk ratio of a 10-year coronary
event for smokers against non-smokers with the same age and sex. A **design**
gathers data that can estimate it. A **causal diagram** says which variables to
adjust for. A **model** turns the data into a number, and the number is
**interpreted** on the scale of the estimand. This page covers the last two
steps: the measures epidemiology uses and how the coefficients of its models
are read. The next pages cover the designs, the diagrams and mediation
[@rothman2021; @hernan2020].

::: {#fig-strategy}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 1.6
boxes <- data.frame(id = c("q", "e", "d", "g", "a", "m", "i"), x = (0:6) * 2.55, y = 0,
                    label = c("Question", "Estimand", "Design", "DAG", "Adjustment\nset", "Model", "Interpretation"),
                    role = c("other", "exposure", "other", "confounder", "confounder", "mediator", "outcome"))
links <- data.frame(from = boxes$id[-7], to = boxes$id[-1])
both(flow_fig, boxes, links, w = 2.0, h = 0.9)
```
From the question to its answer. Each page of this guide covers some of these steps.
:::

## Measures of frequency

| measure | definition | example | typical design |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Prevalence** | proportion of a population that has the condition at a time | 18% of adults have hypertension | cross-sectional |
| **Risk** (cumulative incidence) | proportion of people free of the outcome at the start who develop it over a period | 8% have a coronary event in 10 years | cohort, trial |
| **Rate** (incidence density) | new cases per unit of person-time | 2.5 breast cancers per 1000 woman-years | cohort |
| **Odds** | probability / (1 − probability) | a risk of 0.2 is odds of 0.25 | case-control (only odds ratios) |
| **Hazard** | instantaneous rate among those still at risk at a given time | | cohort with times (Cox) |

Prevalence mixes how often a condition starts and how long it lasts: in a
steady population, **prevalence ≈ incidence rate × mean duration**. A
treatment that keeps patients alive longer *raises* prevalence. A risk always
refers to a period ("10-year risk"), and it requires everyone to be followed
for that period or a method that handles censoring (Kaplan-Meier). When another
event can prevent the outcome (death from other causes before a cancer
relapse), the risk of the outcome is a **cumulative incidence** in the presence
of a **competing event**. One minus Kaplan-Meier, which censors the competing
deaths, overstates it.

## Measures of association

| measure | definition | estimated by |
|---|---|---|
| Risk difference (RD) | risk~1~ − risk~0~ | cohort, trial (2×2 table, binomial model with identity link) |
| Number needed to treat (NNT) | 1 / \|RD\| | trial |
| Risk ratio (RR) | risk~1~ / risk~0~ | cohort, trial, cross-sectional (prevalence ratio) |
| Rate ratio (IRR) | rate~1~ / rate~0~ | cohort (Poisson regression with log person-time as offset) |
| Hazard ratio (HR) | hazard~1~ / hazard~0~, assumed constant over time | cohort, trial (Cox regression) |
| Odds ratio (OR) | odds~1~ / odds~0~ | any design; the only one a case-control study gives |
| Mean difference | mean~1~ − mean~0~ | linear regression |
| Ratio of geometric means | exp(mean of log~1~ − mean of log~0~) | linear regression of a log outcome |

Difference measures say how many people are affected, and that is what
decisions need. Ratio measures say how strong the association is, and they are
usually more stable across populations with different baseline risks. Report
both when you can: a risk ratio of 2 means 10 extra cases per 1000 people if
the baseline risk is 1%, and 200 if it is 20%.

### The odds ratio is not a risk ratio

The odds ratio approaches the risk ratio only when the outcome is rare
(@fig-or-rr). A case-control study of a rare disease therefore estimates the
risk (or rate) ratio. A cross-sectional study of a common condition analysed
with logistic regression reports odds ratios that look much stronger than the
prevalence ratios.

::: {#fig-or-rr}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6
or_rr <- function(mode) {
    p <- PAL(mode)
    r0 <- seq(0.005, 0.45, length.out = 200)
    d <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1.5, 2, 3), function(rr) {
        r1 <- pmin(rr * r0, 0.999)
        data.frame(r0 = r0, or = (r1 / (1 - r1)) / (r0 / (1 - r0)), rr = factor(sprintf("RR = %s", rr), levels = sprintf("RR = %s", c(1.5, 2, 3))))
    }))
    ggplot(d, aes(r0, or, colour = rr)) + geom_hline(yintercept = c(1.5, 2, 3), colour = p$faint, linetype = "dashed") +
        geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + scale_colour_manual(values = unname(p$role[c("exposure", "mediator", "outcome")]), name = NULL) +
        scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1, 12)) +
        labs(x = "risk in the unexposed", y = "odds ratio") + theme_plot(mode)
}
both(or_rr)
```
The odds ratio for a fixed risk ratio (dashed lines), by the risk in the unexposed: equal when the outcome is rare, ever larger as it becomes common.
:::

### Conditional and marginal: non-collapsibility

The odds ratio and the hazard ratio have a property that surprises many
people. Suppose a treatment multiplies the odds by 3 in every subgroup of
patients and the subgroups are perfectly balanced between the arms, so nothing
is confounded. The odds ratio of the whole trial is still *smaller* than 3
[@greenland1999b]. Risk differences and risk ratios do not behave this way.

```{r}
strata <- data.frame(group = c("low risk", "high risk"), r0 = c(0.10, 0.60))
odds <- function(r) r / (1 - r); risk <- function(o) o / (1 + o)
strata$r1 <- risk(3 * odds(strata$r0))
m0 <- mean(strata$r0); m1 <- mean(strata$r1)
tab <- rbind(strata, data.frame(group = "whole population (half each)", r0 = m0, r1 = m1))
tab$OR <- odds(tab$r1) / odds(tab$r0); tab$RR <- tab$r1 / tab$r0; tab$RD <- tab$r1 - tab$r0
knitr::kable(transform(tab, r0 = round(r0, 3), r1 = round(r1, 3), OR = round(OR, 2), RR = round(RR, 2), RD = round(RD, 3)),
             col.names = c("", "risk, control", "risk, treated", "OR", "RR", "RD"), row.names = FALSE)
```

Both subgroups have an odds ratio of 3, and the whole population has
`r round(odds(m1) / odds(m0), 2)`. Neither number is wrong: they answer
different questions. The **conditional** odds ratio is the effect for a patient
with given characteristics; the **marginal** one is the effect on the
population. In a trial the crude analysis estimates the marginal effect and an
analysis adjusted for prognostic variables the conditional one, which is
further from 1. studysim generates data with conditional effects, and its
answer key shows both for trials (*absolute effects in the trial*).

```{r}
trial_table("indomethacin_ercp", "pancreatitis")
```

## Models and how to read their coefficients

| outcome | model | exp(β) or β is | jamovi |
|---|---|---|---|
| continuous | linear regression | β: difference in the mean per unit of x | *Regression ▸ Linear Regression* |
| continuous, skewed | linear regression of log(y) | exp(β): ratio of geometric means | *Compute* log(y), then linear regression |
| binary | logistic regression | odds ratio | *Regression ▸ Logistic Regression ▸ 2 Outcomes* |
| binary, matched sets | conditional logistic regression | odds ratio within sets | **condLogReg** |
| count or rate | Poisson (negative binomial) regression, log person-time as offset | rate ratio | **GAMLj** |
| time to event | Cox regression | hazard ratio | **prognosis** |

The same rules apply to every model:

- **A coefficient is the effect of its variable with the other variables in the
  model held fixed.** It is a *conditional* effect. Whether it is the effect you
  want depends on which variables are in the model: the
  [causal diagram](guide-dags.qmd) decides that, not the model.
- **Per unit.** A coefficient for age is *per year*. A hazard ratio of 1.05 per
  year is 1.05^10^ = 1.63 per 10 years. Choose units that make sense: per 10
  mmHg, per 5 kg/m², per standard deviation.
- **Per level.** A categorical variable gets one coefficient per level, each
  against the reference level. Changing the reference changes the numbers but
  not the model.
- **Log scale.** Logistic, Poisson and Cox coefficients are logarithms: exp(β)
  is the ratio, and effects of several variables multiply. A log-transformed
  exposure gives the effect per doubling (log~2~) or per tenfold increase (log~10~).
- **Interaction.** With a product term X × Z, the coefficient of X is the effect
  of X *when Z is at its reference or zero*, and the interaction coefficient is
  how much that effect changes per unit of Z. If zero is not a meaningful value
  of Z (a BMI of zero), centre Z first, or the main effects become meaningless.
  This is the problem studysim's `center:` solves in its own scenarios.
- **The intercept** is the outcome (or its log odds or log rate) when every
  variable is at zero or its reference: rarely of interest, and meaningless
  without centring.
- **Categorising a continuous variable** loses information and leaves residual
  confounding within the categories. It is useful for showing a shape (dose
  response), not for adjustment.
- **Small numbers.** Logistic and Cox models need roughly ten events per
  parameter; with fewer, coefficients are unstable and biased away from the
  null [@peduzzi1996]. studysim warns when a study falls short.

### What studysim's answer key reports

| column | estimand |
|---|---|
| *Direct (conditional)* | the effect in the generating model, every other variable fixed |
| *Total* | the effect of changing the variable while its consequences change too, given the variables it does not cause ([Causal diagrams](guide-dags.qmd)) |
| *Crude* | the association without adjustment |
| *Adjusted (all)* | the conditional association given every measured variable |
| *Adjusted (DAG)* | the association given the measured variables that the diagram says to adjust for |
| *Absolute effects* (trials) | risks per arm, RD, NNT, marginal and conditional OR or HR |

## Effect modification and interaction

### Two words, two questions

- **Effect modification**: the effect of an exposure X *differs between groups*
  of another variable Z. The effect of BMI on breast cancer is protective before
  menopause and harmful after it. Z need not cause anything: it describes in whom
  X acts more strongly.
- **Interaction**: the *joint* effect of two exposures is not what their separate
  effects predict. Smoking and asbestos together cause far more lung cancer than
  the two separately would suggest. Both are causes, and the question is what
  happens if we act on both.

They are estimated the same way (X within levels of Z, or a product term X × Z),
and the words are often used interchangeably. The distinction matters when
deciding what to do: a modifier tells you *who* benefits most from acting on X.

### It depends on the scale

Whether an effect "differs" depends on how effects are measured. In this example,
exposure X triples the risk both in people without and with a second factor Z:

```{r}
r <- c(r00 = 0.01, r10 = 0.03, r01 = 0.05, r11 = 0.15)
knitr::kable(data.frame(group = c("Z absent", "Z present"), unexposed = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * r[c(1, 3)]),
                        exposed = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * r[c(2, 4)]), RR = r[c(2, 4)] / r[c(1, 3)],
                        RD = sprintf("%+.0f%%", 100 * (r[c(2, 4)] - r[c(1, 3)]))),
             col.names = c("", "risk, X absent", "risk, X present", "risk ratio of X", "risk difference of X"), row.names = FALSE)
```

On the **ratio** scale there is no modification: the risk ratio is 3 in both
groups. On the **difference** scale there is a great deal: X adds 2 cases per
100 people without Z and 10 per 100 with Z (@fig-scale). Whenever two factors
both act, no modification on one scale implies modification on the other.

::: {#fig-scale}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.4
library(patchwork)
scale_fig <- function(mode) {
    p <- PAL(mode)
    d <- data.frame(x = factor(rep(c("X absent", "X present"), 2), levels = c("X absent", "X present")),
                    z = rep(c("Z absent", "Z present"), each = 2), risk = unname(r[c("r00", "r10", "r01", "r11")]))
    cols <- c(`Z absent` = p$role[["exposure"]], `Z present` = p$role[["outcome"]])
    base <- ggplot(d, aes(x, risk, colour = z, group = z)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 3) +
        scale_colour_manual(values = cols, name = NULL) + labs(x = NULL) + theme_plot(mode)
    a <- base + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.16)) +
        labs(y = "risk", title = "Difference scale: lines diverge") +
        annotate("text", x = 2.08, y = c(0.03, 0.15), label = c("+2%", "+10%"), hjust = 0, colour = p$fg, size = 3.6)
    b <- base + scale_y_log10(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0.008, 0.2)) +
        labs(y = "risk (log scale)", title = "Ratio scale: lines parallel") +
        annotate("text", x = 2.08, y = c(0.03, 0.15), label = c("x3", "x3"), hjust = 0, colour = p$fg, size = 3.6)
    (a + b + plot_layout(guides = "collect")) & theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(size = 11, colour = p$fg))
}
both(scale_fig)
```
The same four risks on a difference scale (left) and on a ratio scale (right): no interaction on the multiplicative scale, a strong one on the additive scale.
:::

Logistic and Cox models are multiplicative: their product term tests departure
from multiplying the effects. Public health usually cares about the additive
scale, because it counts cases: here, removing X prevents five times more cases
among people with Z. The **relative excess risk due to interaction**,
RERI = RR~11~ − RR~10~ − RR~01~ + 1, measures additive interaction from ratio
measures: here 15 − 3 − 5 + 1 = `r unname(r["r11"] / r["r00"] - r["r10"] / r["r00"] - r["r01"] / r["r00"] + 1)`
(0 means no additive interaction).

### Reading a model with a product term

In a model `logit(risk) = β0 + β1·X + β2·Z + β3·X·Z`:

| coefficient | is | holds |
|---|---|---|
| exp(β1) | odds ratio of X | when Z = 0 (its reference level) |
| exp(β2) | odds ratio of Z | when X = 0 |
| exp(β3) | ratio of the odds ratios of X between Z = 1 and Z = 0 | the multiplicative interaction |
| exp(β1 + β3) | odds ratio of X | when Z = 1 |

The "main effects" are therefore not average effects: each is the effect at the
reference or zero of the other variable. When the other variable is continuous
and zero is meaningless, a main effect is an extrapolation far from the data.
Centre the continuous variable first (subtract a typical value), so that the
main effect of the modifier holds at that typical value.

*Breast cancer risk factors*: the effect of BMI is modified by menopause
(per 5 kg/m², HR 0.93 before and 1.12 after). The table fits the same
interaction model to a large simulated case-control study, with BMI as it is and
centred at the population mean.

```{r}
sc_b <- load_scenario(lib, "breast_cancer_risk")
cc <- simulate_study(sc_b, "breast_cancer", "case_control", 14000, sc_b$order, seed = 4, key = FALSE)$data_raw
cen <- sc_b$outcomes$breast_cancer$effects$bmi$center
cc$bmi5 <- cc$bmi / 5; cc$bmi5c <- (cc$bmi - cen) / 5
f0 <- glm(case ~ age + hrt + bmi5 * menopause, binomial(), cc)
f1 <- glm(case ~ age + hrt + bmi5c * menopause, binomial(), cc)
b0 <- coef(f0); b1 <- coef(f1)
row <- function(lab, a, b) data.frame(term = lab, raw = sprintf("%.2f", a), centred = sprintf("%.2f", b))
knitr::kable(rbind(
    row("BMI per 5 kg/m², before menopause (exp β1)", exp(b0[["bmi5"]]), exp(b1[["bmi5c"]])),
    row("BMI per 5 kg/m², after menopause (exp(β1 + β3))", exp(b0[["bmi5"]] + b0[["bmi5:menopausepost"]]), exp(b1[["bmi5c"]] + b1[["bmi5c:menopausepost"]])),
    row("ratio of the two (exp β3)", exp(b0[["bmi5:menopausepost"]]), exp(b1[["bmi5c:menopausepost"]])),
    row("menopause, post vs pre (exp β2)", exp(b0[["menopausepost"]]), exp(b1[["menopausepost"]]))),
    col.names = c("", "BMI as measured", sprintf("BMI centred at %.1f", cen)), row.names = FALSE)
```

The BMI effects and their ratio do not change with centring. The "effect of
menopause" does: with BMI as measured it is the odds ratio at a BMI of 0, which
nobody has (@fig-centring). Centred, it is the odds ratio at a typical BMI, which
is what the question means.

::: {#fig-centring}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
bm <- seq(0, 45, length.out = 200)
lp <- function(post) b0[["bmi5"]] * bm / 5 + post * (b0[["menopausepost"]] + b0[["bmi5:menopausepost"]] * bm / 5)
cdat <- rbind(data.frame(bmi = bm, or = exp(lp(0) - lp(0)[which.min(abs(bm - cen))]), status = "before menopause"),
              data.frame(bmi = bm, or = exp(lp(1) - lp(0)[which.min(abs(bm - cen))]), status = "after menopause"))
cent_fig <- function(mode) {
    p <- PAL(mode)
    g0 <- cdat$or[cdat$status == "after menopause"][1]; g1 <- cdat$or[cdat$status == "before menopause"][1]
    ggplot(cdat, aes(bmi, or, colour = status)) +
        annotate("rect", xmin = 16, xmax = 48, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = p$faint, alpha = 0.35) +
        geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + scale_y_log10() +
        annotate("segment", x = 0.6, xend = 0.6, y = g1, yend = g0, colour = p$fg, arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"), ends = "both")) +
        annotate("text", x = 1.4, y = sqrt(g0 * g1), hjust = 0, colour = p$fg, size = 3.4, label = "exp(β2) with BMI as measured:\nthe gap at BMI 0") +
        annotate("segment", x = cen, xend = cen, y = 0.7, yend = 1.4, colour = p$fg, linetype = "dashed") +
        annotate("text", x = cen + 0.8, y = 1.45, hjust = 0, colour = p$fg, size = 3.4, label = "centred: the gap\nat a typical BMI") +
        annotate("text", x = 40, y = 0.48, label = "where the data are", colour = p$muted, size = 3.4) +
        coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.45, 1.9)) +
        scale_colour_manual(values = c(`before menopause` = p$role[["exposure"]], `after menopause` = p$role[["outcome"]]), name = NULL) +
        labs(x = "body mass index (kg/m2)", y = "relative odds (log scale)") + theme_plot(mode)
}
both(cent_fig)
```
The fitted interaction model: the two lines cross near the mean BMI. The main effect of menopause is the vertical gap between them at BMI 0 (left arrow), far outside the data (shaded), when BMI is used as measured; after centring it is the gap at a typical BMI.
:::

### A modifier that reverses the effect

*Dexamethasone in hospitalised COVID-19* (RECOVERY): dexamethasone lowers
mortality in patients on oxygen or ventilation, but not in those without
respiratory support. This is **qualitative** modification: the effect changes
direction. Its overall odds ratio, averaged over the patients of the trial, would
hide both the harm and the largest benefit.

::: {#fig-recovery}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3
sc_r <- load_scenario(lib, "recovery_dexamethasone")
tr <- simulate_study(sc_r, "death_28d", "rct", 30000, sc_r$order, seed = 2, key = FALSE)$data_raw
or_of <- function(d) { f <- glm(death_28d ~ treatment + age + sex + diabetes, binomial(), d); b <- coef(f)[["treatmentdexamethasone"]]
    se <- sqrt(vcov(f)["treatmentdexamethasone", "treatmentdexamethasone"]); exp(b + c(0, -1.96, 1.96) * se) }
st <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(tr$support), function(l) data.frame(group = l, t(or_of(tr[tr$support == l, ])))))
st <- rbind(st, data.frame(group = "all patients", t(or_of(tr))))
names(st)[2:4] <- c("or", "lo", "hi")
st$truth <- c(1.38, 0.80, 0.55, NA)
st$group <- factor(st$group, levels = rev(st$group))
rec_fig <- function(mode) {
    p <- PAL(mode)
    ggplot(st, aes(y = group)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = p$muted, linetype = "dashed") +
        geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.2, colour = p$role[["exposure"]]) +
        geom_point(aes(x = or), size = 3, colour = p$role[["exposure"]]) +
        geom_point(aes(x = truth), shape = 4, size = 3.5, stroke = 1.2, colour = p$role[["outcome"]], na.rm = TRUE) +
        scale_x_log10() + labs(x = "odds ratio of death, dexamethasone vs usual care (log scale)", y = "respiratory support") + theme_plot(mode)
}
both(rec_fig)
```
Odds ratios of death in a simulated RECOVERY trial of 30,000 patients, by respiratory support (dots and 95% CI) and the true values (crosses): harm without support, benefit growing with the severity. The odds ratio of all patients averages them.
:::

### In practice

- **Decide in advance** which modifiers to examine and why (biology, previous
  evidence). Testing many subgroups guarantees false positives.
- **Report the effect within each group**, with its confidence interval, and the
  test of interaction. A significant effect in one subgroup and a non-significant
  one in another is not evidence that they differ: compare them with the
  interaction test.
- **Interaction tests have little power**: detecting an interaction as large as
  the main effect needs about four times the sample size. A non-significant test
  does not show that the effect is the same.
- **Say which scale** you used, and give the additive measures (RD, RERI) when
  the question is about how many cases could be prevented.

**In jamovi**: in *Regression* models, select both variables in *Model Builder*
and add their interaction (centre a continuous modifier first with *Compute*);
*Frequencies ▸ Independent Samples* with the modifier as *Layer* gives the odds
ratio in each group and a test of homogeneity; the **prognosis** module gives
subgroup hazard ratios for an interaction in a Cox model, and **GAMLj** *simple
effects*. **In studysim**: *Breast cancer risk factors* (BMI × menopause),
*Dexamethasone in hospitalised COVID-19* (treatment × respiratory support),
*HPV and cofactors of cervical cancer (IARC multicentric)* (cofactors that act only with HPV), and the 2×2
factorial design with an *interaction* between the two treatments.
